imo-2009-01.title: Work modulo each prime power
imo-2009-01.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that also $n\mid a_k(a_1-1)$. Write $a_{k+1}=a_1$, so $n\mid a_i(a_{i+1}-1)$ for all $i=1,\dots,k$ (indices cyclic). Note $n\ge2$, since $\{1,\dots,n\}$ contains $k\ge2$ distinct numbers.

Let $q=p^e$ be a prime power exactly dividing $n$. For each $i$, $q\mid a_i(a_{i+1}-1)$. A number and its predecessor cannot both be divisible by $p$; so if $p\mid a_i$ then $\gcd(q,a_i-1)=1$, and if $p\mid a_{i+1}-1$ then $\gcd(q,a_{i+1})=1$.

- **If $p\mid a_1$.** Then $p\nmid a_1-1$, so from $q\mid a_k(a_1-1)$ we get $q\mid a_k$. Then $p\nmid a_k-1$ and $q\mid a_{k-1}(a_k-1)$ gives $q\mid a_{k-1}$, and so on backwards: $a_i\equiv0\pmod q$ for all $i$.
- **If $p\nmid a_1$.** Then $q\mid a_1(a_2-1)$ gives $q\mid a_2-1$; so $p\nmid a_2$ and $q\mid a_2(a_3-1)$ gives $q\mid a_3-1$; continuing, $a_2\equiv a_3\equiv\dots\equiv a_k\equiv1\pmod q$, and finally $p\nmid a_k$ with $q\mid a_k(a_1-1)$ gives $a_1\equiv1\pmod q$.

Either way all $a_i$ are congruent modulo $q$. As this holds for every prime power exactly dividing $n$, the Chinese remainder theorem gives $a_1\equiv a_2\equiv\dots\equiv a_k\pmod n$. But they are distinct elements of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $k\ge2$ — contradiction. ∎

imo-2009-02.title: Power of a point and a similarity
imo-2009-02.body:
Let $R$ be the circumradius.

**Reduction.** $P$ is inside chord $CA$ of the circumcircle, so its power is $OP^2-R^2=-PA\cdot PC$; similarly $OQ^2-R^2=-QA\cdot QB$. Hence $OP=OQ$ iff $AP\cdot PC=AQ\cdot QB$.

**Midlines.** In triangle $PQB$, $M,K$ are midpoints of $PQ,PB$, so $MK\parallel QB$ (i.e. $\parallel AB$) and $MK=\frac{QB}{2}$. In triangle $QPC$, $M,L$ are midpoints of $QP,QC$, so $ML\parallel PC$ (i.e. $\parallel AC$) and $ML=\frac{PC}{2}$.

**Similarity.** The line $PQ$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $M$. By the tangent–chord angle, the angle between $PQ$ and the chord $MK$ equals the inscribed angle $\angle MLK$, and the angle between $PQ$ and the chord $ML$ equals $\angle MKL$. Since $MK\parallel QA$ and $ML\parallel PA$, the first is the angle of triangle $APQ$ at $Q$ and the second its angle at $P$:
$$\angle AQP=\angle MLK,\qquad \angle APQ=\angle MKL .$$
(With directed angles this reads $\measuredangle(QP,QA)=\measuredangle(LM,LK)$ and $\measuredangle(PQ,PA)=\measuredangle(KM,KL)$, valid in every configuration; the triangles are oppositely similar.) So triangles $APQ$ and $MKL$ are similar with $A\leftrightarrow M$, $P\leftrightarrow K$, $Q\leftrightarrow L$, and
$$\frac{AP}{AQ}=\frac{MK}{ML}=\frac{QB/2}{PC/2}=\frac{QB}{PC}.$$
Thus $AP\cdot PC=AQ\cdot QB$, and $OP=OQ$. ∎

imo-2009-03.title: Extremal gaps (Alex Zhai's argument)
imo-2009-03.body:
Write $s(n)=s_n$ and $d_n=s(n+1)-s(n)\ge1$. Let
$$s(s(n))=Dn+A,\qquad s(s(n)+1)=D'n+B .$$

**Same common difference.** Since $s(n)<s(n)+1\le s(n+1)$ and $s$ is increasing,
$$Dn+A=s(s(n))<s(s(n)+1)=D'n+B\le s(s(n+1))=Dn+D+A$$
for all $n$. Dividing by $n$ and letting $n\to\infty$ gives $D'=D$.

**Bounded gaps.** For integers $u<v$, $s(v)-s(u)\ge v-u$ (strictly increasing integers). Hence $d_n=s(n+1)-s(n)\le s(s(n+1))-s(s(n))=D$. So the positive integers $d_n$ are bounded and attain a maximum $\overline m$ and a minimum $\underline m$.

**Key identity.** For any $a$, the numbers $j$ with $s(s(a))\le j<s(s(a+1))$ are $D$ consecutive integers, and
$$\sum_{j=s(s(a))}^{s(s(a+1))-1}d_j=s\bigl(s(s(a+1))\bigr)-s\bigl(s(s(a))\bigr)=\bigl(D\,s(a+1)+A\bigr)-\bigl(D\,s(a)+A\bigr)=D\,d_a,$$
using $s(s(m))=Dm+A$ with $m=s(a+1)$ and $m=s(a)$. Also, using both progressions with $n=s(a)$,
$$d_{s(s(a))}=s\bigl(s(s(a))+1\bigr)-s\bigl(s(s(a))\bigr)=\bigl(D\,s(a)+B\bigr)-\bigl(D\,s(a)+A\bigr)=B-A .$$

**Conclusion.** Choose $a$ with $d_a=\overline m$. The $D$ terms in the sum are each $\le\overline m$ and add up to $D\overline m$, so all equal $\overline m$; in particular $d_{s(s(a))}=\overline m$, so $\overline m=B-A$. Choosing $a$ with $d_a=\underline m$, the same argument (each term $\ge\underline m$) gives $\underline m=B-A$. Thus $\overline m=\underline m$, all gaps $d_n$ are equal, and $s$ is an arithmetic progression. ∎

imo-2009-04.title: Law of sines in triangle IEC
imo-2009-04.body:
Let $\angle CAB=4x$ with $0^\circ<x<45^\circ$, so $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=90^\circ-2x$. Let $I$ be the incentre of $ABC$; it lies on $AD$ and on $BE$, with $I$ between $B$ and $E$. Since $AB=AC$, $AD\perp BC$.

**Locating $K$.** $K$ lies on the bisector of $\angle ACD$, which is line $CI$, and between $C$ and $I$ (as $I$ lies on side $AD$ of triangle $ADC$). Also $DK$ bisects the right angle $\angle IDC$. In the right triangle $IDC$, the angle bisector theorem gives
$$\frac{IK}{KC}=\frac{DI}{DC}=\tan\angle ICD=\tan(45^\circ-x).$$

**Angles in triangle $IEC$.** $\angle ECI=45^\circ-x$; $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{4x}{2}=90^\circ+2x$, so $\angle EIC=90^\circ-2x$; hence $\angle IEC=45^\circ+3x$. Since ray $EB$ = ray $EI$, $\angle BEK=\angle IEK=:\theta\in(0,45^\circ+3x)$, and $\angle KEC=45^\circ+3x-\theta$. By the law of sines in triangles $IEK$ and $KEC$,
$$\frac{IK}{KC}=\frac{EK\sin\theta/\sin(90^\circ-2x)}{EK\sin(45^\circ+3x-\theta)/\sin(45^\circ-x)}=\frac{\sin(45^\circ-x)}{\cos2x}\cdot\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin(45^\circ+3x-\theta)} .$$
The factor $\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin(c-\theta)}$ ($c=45^\circ+3x<180^\circ$) is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $(0,c)$, so $\theta=45^\circ$ holds **iff** the value of this expression at $\theta=45^\circ$ equals $\tan(45^\circ-x)$:
$$\frac{\sin(45^\circ-x)\sin45^\circ}{\cos2x\,\sin3x}=\frac{\sin(45^\circ-x)}{\cos(45^\circ-x)}\iff \sin45^\circ\cos(45^\circ-x)=\sin3x\cos2x .$$

**Solving.** Write $\cos(45^\circ-x)=\sin(45^\circ+x)$ and $\cos2x=\sin(90^\circ-2x)$. By product-to-sum, $\sin45^\circ\sin(45^\circ+x)=\frac12\bigl(\cos x-\cos(90^\circ+x)\bigr)$ and $\sin3x\sin(90^\circ-2x)=\frac12\bigl(\cos(5x-90^\circ)-\cos(90^\circ+x)\bigr)$. So the condition is $\cos x=\cos(5x-90^\circ)$, i.e.
$$0=\cos(5x-90^\circ)-\cos x=-2\sin(3x-45^\circ)\sin(2x-45^\circ).$$
For $0^\circ<x<45^\circ$: $3x-45^\circ\in(-45^\circ,90^\circ)$ vanishes only at $x=15^\circ$, and $2x-45^\circ\in(-45^\circ,45^\circ)$ only at $x=22.5^\circ$. Since every step was an equivalence, exactly these work: $\angle CAB=4x=60^\circ$ or $90^\circ$.

**Answer:** $\angle CAB=60^\circ$ or $90^\circ$.

imo-2009-05.title: $f(1)=1$, involution, then an arithmetic progression
imo-2009-05.body:
**The identity works:** sides $a$, $b$, $a+b-1$ satisfy $a+b>a+b-1$, $b+(a+b-1)>a$ and $a+(a+b-1)>b$.

Now let $f$ satisfy the condition; "triangle" means all three strict triangle inequalities.

**Step 1: $f(1)=1$.** With $a=1$: $1,\ f(b),\ f(b+f(1)-1)$ form a triangle, so $|f(b)-f(b+f(1)-1)|<1$, i.e. $f(b)=f(b+f(1)-1)$ for all $b$. If $N=f(1)-1\ge1$, $f$ is periodic with period $N$, hence bounded by some $C$; but $a=2C$ would need $2C<f(b)+f(b+f(a)-1)\le2C$. So $f(1)=1$.

**Step 2: $f(f(a))=a$.** With $b=1$: $a,\ 1,\ f(f(a))$ form a triangle, so $|a-f(f(a))|<1$. Hence $f$ is a bijection.

**Step 3.** Let $\delta=f(2)-1$; $\delta\ge1$ because $f(2)\ne f(1)$. Take $a=2$, $b=f(n)$: the sides are $2$, $f(f(n))=n$ and $f(f(n)+\delta)=:y$. So $|n-y|<2$, i.e. $y\in\{n-1,n,n+1\}$, and $f(y)=f(f(f(n)+\delta))=f(n)+\delta$. If $y=n$ then $\delta=0$, impossible. Hence
$$f(n+1)=f(n)+\delta\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(n\ge2\ \text{and}\ f(n-1)=f(n)+\delta\bigr).$$

**Step 4: $f(n)=1+(n-1)\delta$ for all $n$.** True for $n=1,2$. If it holds up to $n\ge2$, then $f(n-1)=1+(n-2)\delta\ne1+n\delta=f(n)+\delta$, so Step 3 forces $f(n+1)=f(n)+\delta=1+n\delta$.

**Step 5.** Finally $2=f(f(2))=f(1+\delta)=1+\delta^2$, so $\delta=1$ and $f(n)=n$ for all $n$. ∎

imo-2009-06.title: Strong induction on the number of jumps
imo-2009-06.body:
Call the points of $M$ *mines*. We prove by strong induction on $n$ the statement

> $(\mathcal S_n)$: for distinct positive integers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ with sum $s$ and any set $M$ of **at most** $n-1$ positive integers with $s\notin M$, some order of the jumps avoids $M$.

(Only mines in $(0,s)$ matter.) For $n=1$ there are no mines. Let $n\ge2$, assume $\mathcal S_1,\dots,\mathcal S_{n-1}$, order $a_1<\dots<a_n$, and put $x=s-a_n$, the sum of the $n-1$ shorter jumps.

**Case 1: $x\notin M$ and some mine is greater than $x$.** Then at most $n-2$ mines lie in $(0,x)$. By $\mathcal S_{n-1}$, jumps $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ reach $x$ avoiding them; then jump $a_n$ to $s\notin M$.

**Case 2: all mines are $\le x$** (and $M\ne\varnothing$; otherwise any order works). Let $m=\max M$ and $M'=M\setminus\{m\}$, which has at most $n-2$ elements and does not contain $x$ (if $x\in M$ then $x=m$). By $\mathcal S_{n-1}$, jumps $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ in some order reach $x$ landing at $p_1<p_2<\dots<p_{n-1}=x$, none in $M'$. If no $p_j$ equals $m$, finish with $a_n$. Otherwise $p_j=m$ for one $j$, reached by a jump of length $a_r$. Make jump $a_n$ in place of that jump and postpone $a_r$ to the very end. The landing points become $p_1,\dots,p_{j-1}$ (all $<m$ and not in $M'$, so safe), then $p_i+(a_n-a_r)$ for $i=j,\dots,n-1$, which are all $>p_j=m$ and hence exceed every mine, and finally $s$. This order avoids $M$.

**Case 3: $x\in M$ and some mine is greater than $x$.** Then at most $n-3$ mines lie in $(0,x)$, so $n\ge3$. Consider $i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ and the points
$$s-a_i\in(x,s),\qquad y_i=s-a_i-a_n=x-a_i\in(0,x).$$
For different $i$ these points are different. Let $r$ and $t$ be the numbers of mines in $(x,s)$ and in $(0,x)$; since $x$ is also a mine, $r+t\le n-2$. Each mine in $(x,s)$ equals $s-a_i$ for at most one $i$, and each mine in $(0,x)$ equals $y_i$ for at most one $i$, so at most $n-2$ indices $i$ are spoiled; choose an $i$ with $s-a_i\notin M$ and $y_i\notin M$. The $n-2$ jumps other than $a_i,a_n$ have sum $y_i\notin M$, and at most $t\le n-3$ mines lie below $y_i$; by $\mathcal S_{n-2}$ they reach $y_i$ safely. Then jump $a_n$ to $s-a_i$ (safe) and $a_i$ to $s$.

These cases cover everything (if $x\notin M$, Case 1 or 2; if $x\in M$, Case 2 or 3), completing the induction. Applying $\mathcal S_n$ with $|M|=n-1$ solves the problem. ∎
